answer.worked:
By Pythagoras, the hypotenuse is $h=\sqrt{1^2+2^2}=\sqrt5$.

$$\begin{align*}
\sin\theta&=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac1{\sqrt5}\\
\cos\theta&=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{hypotenuse}}=\frac2{\sqrt5}\\
\tan\theta&=\frac{\text{opposite}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac12\\
\csc\theta&=\frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{opposite}}=\sqrt5\\
\sec\theta&=\frac{\text{hypotenuse}}{\text{adjacent}}=\frac{\sqrt5}{2}\\
\cot\theta&=\frac{\text{adjacent}}{\text{opposite}}=2.
\end{align*}$$

answer.worked: $$\begin{align*}\tan\theta\cos\theta&=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cos\theta\\\tan\theta\cos\theta&=\sin\theta\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\cot\theta\sin\theta&=\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\sin\theta\\\cot\theta\sin\theta&=\cos\theta\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\sin\theta\sec\theta&=\sin\theta\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\\\sin\theta\sec\theta&=\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\\\sin\theta\sec\theta&=\tan\theta\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\csc\theta\cos\theta&=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\cos\theta\\\csc\theta\cos\theta&=\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\\\csc\theta\cos\theta&=\cot\theta\end{align*}$$
$$\begin{align*}\frac{\cot\theta}{\csc\theta}&=\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\times\sin\theta\\\frac{\cot\theta}{\csc\theta}&=\cos\theta\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta}&=\frac{1}{\cos\theta}\times\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\\\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta}&=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\\\frac{\sec\theta}{\tan\theta}&=\csc\theta\end{align*}$$

$$\begin{align*}\frac{\csc\theta}{\sec\theta}&=\frac{1}{\sin\theta}\times\cos\theta\\\frac{\csc\theta}{\sec\theta}&=\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\\\frac{\csc\theta}{\sec\theta}&=\cot\theta\end{align*}$$
$$\frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}=\cot\theta$$

Use the symmetry and period of cosine.

By the symmetry and period of cosine, either
$$\begin{align*}3x&=2x+2k\pi\\x&=2k\pi\end{align*}$$
or
$$\begin{align*}3x&=-2x+2k\pi\\5x&=2k\pi\\x&=\frac{2k\pi}{5}.\end{align*}$$
Restricting to $[0,2\pi]$ and removing duplicates gives

answer.short:

Use the symmetry and period of sine.
answer.worked:
By the symmetry and period of sine, either
$$\begin{align*}4x&=3x+2k\pi\\x&=2k\pi\end{align*}$$
or
$$\begin{align*}4x&=\pi-3x+2k\pi\\7x&=(2k+1)\pi\\x&=\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{7}.\end{align*}$$
Within $[0,2\pi]$, the first case gives $0,2\pi$ and the second uses $k=0,1,\ldots,6$. Hence
$$x=0,\frac{\pi}{7},\frac{3\pi}{7},\frac{5\pi}{7},\pi,\frac{9\pi}{7},\frac{11\pi}{7},\frac{13\pi}{7},2\pi.$$

Using $\cos 2x=1-2\sin^2x$,
$$\begin{align*}\sin x&=1-2\sin^2x\\2\sin^2x+\sin x-1&=0\\(2\sin x-1)(\sin x+1)&=0.\end{align*}$$
Thus $\sin x=\tfrac12$ or $\sin x=-1$. The reference angle for $\tfrac12$ is $\tfrac{\pi}{6}$, with sine positive in Quadrants I and II. Therefore
$$x=\frac{\pi}{6},\frac{5\pi}{6},\frac{3\pi}{2}.$$

content.prompt: Find the values of $c$ for which the graph of $y=\sin x$ is tangent to the graph of $y=\cos x+c$ at exactly one point in the interval $[0,2\pi]$.

answer.short:
$c=\pm\sqrt2$.

These are the maximum and minimum values of $\sin x-\cos x$.
answer.worked:
At an intersection,
$$\begin{align*}\sin x&=\cos x+c\\\sin x-\cos x&=c.\end{align*}$$
On the unit circle, write $X=\cos x$ and $Y=\sin x$. The equation $Y-X=c$ represents parallel lines of gradient $1$. A line touches the unit circle once when its perpendicular distance from the centre equals the radius:
$$\begin{align*}\frac{|c|}{\sqrt{1^2+(-1)^2}}&=1\\|c|&=\sqrt2.\end{align*}$$
Thus the difference $\sin x-\cos x$ has maximum $\sqrt2$ at $x=\frac{3\pi}{4}$ and minimum $-\sqrt2$ at $x=\frac{7\pi}{4}$. Each occurs once in $[0,2\pi]$. At either extremum the two graphs touch without crossing, so
$$c=\pm\sqrt2.$$

Such a triangle is composed of a right angle and two acute angles, one of which is labelled with the Greek letter θ (theta). The side opposite the right angle is called the hypotenuse. entries.description: The unit circle and the circular functions

entries.description: We extend the definition of the trigonometric ratios to all angles using the unit circle. A radius from the origin forms an angle θ, measured anticlockwise from the positive x-axis, and intersects the unit circle at P(x, y). This angle can be expressed in degrees or, preferably, radians. We now define sin(θ) to be the y-coordinate of the point P, and cos(θ) to be the x-coordinate of the point P. This agrees with our previous definition of the trigonometric ratios when the angle is acute, but also allows them to be defined for any angle. Due to their connection with the unit circle, these extensions of the trigonometric ratios are called circular functions.
